title: Final Project Guidelines
text:
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics


Each student will write a short (3–5 page) scientific paper supported by an analysis of either real or simulated data using one of the models covered during this semester. The paper will be submitted along with a self-contained R script (or .qmd or .Rmd file), and data.





Briefly describe the motivation, methods, results, and implications.



Describe motivation for the study and background information. Cite prior research.



Describe study area, study species, study design, data collection, and data analysis. Emphasize the model description and include equations.



Describe key findings, and support them with references to figures and tables.



Explain how your results advance knowledge and inform conservation efforts. Connect your results to previously published work.



Use any peer-reviewed journal format you like, and be consistent.



Include at least 1 table and 2 figures, along with clear, informative captions.





Sept 25: Email instructors with brief (1 paragraph) description of project idea
Oct 20: Submit first draft (later than the syllabus says)
Oct 20–Nov 21: Meet with Dr. Chandler to discuss first draft
Nov 3: Submit peer review
Nov 17 & Nov 19: Presentations
Dec 1: Submit final paper, code, and data




The project comprises 30% of your overall grade, and will be graded as follows:

First draft: 10%

No Results or Discussion required, but you must submit an R script.
The analysis does not need to be complete, but you should make substantial progress.

Meeting with Dr. Chandler: 10%
Peer review: 10%

Write your review as you would for a peer-reviewed journal. Good advice can be found here and here.
Each of your two reviews should be 1-2 pages, including sections for “general comments” and “specific comments.”

Final paper: 60%

Graded using criteria listed above under “Paper structure”. It should also incorporate suggestions from peer-review and from the presentations.

Analysis: 10%

R code should be easy to follow and annotated
We should be able to reproduce results reported in the paper
Script should not throw errors
Script should not include lengthy data formatting code. Format the data elsewhere, and then import it ready for analysis.


The 10-min presentation counts towards an additional 20% of your overall grade. The presentation should include background information, methods, results, and conclusions.

Course Description
Recently developed statistical tools make it possible to fit models of population dynamics to field data while accounting for observation error. This course will explain how to use these tools for statistical inference and prediction about animal population parameters including abundance, occupancy, survival, recruitment, and dispersal.


Course Objectives and Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students will know how to (1) design studies of wildlife population dynamics, (2) fit statistical models to data collected in the field, (3) interpret results, and (4) make predictions useful for informing conservation decisions.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Overview

The objectives are the same as with binomial \(N\)-mixture models.

Estimate abundance
Model spatial variation in abundance/density


The difference is that, instead of repeated count data at each site, we have data from sampling methods such as:

Double observer sampling
Removal sampling
Mark-recapture
Distance sampling
And other methods that yield multinomial counts

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Multinomial \(N\)-mixture model

State model (with Poisson assumption) \[
  \mathrm{log}(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \beta_2 {\color{blue} x_{i2}} + \cdots \\
  N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
\]
Observation model \[
  \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \alpha_2 {\color{Purple} w_{ij}} + \cdots \\
  \{y_{i1}, \dots, y_{iK}\}  \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N_i, \pi(p_{i1}, \dots, p_{iJ}))
\]
Definitions


\(\lambda_i\) – Expected value of abundance at site \(i\)  \(N_i\) – Realized value of abundance at site \(i\)  \(p_{ij}\) – Probability of detecting an individual at site \(i\) on occasion \(j\)  \(\pi(p)\) – Function mapping \(J\) detection probs to \(K\) multinomial cell probs  \(y_{ik}\) – Multinomial count data (The final count is not observed!)  \(\color{blue} x_1\) and \(\color{blue} x_2\) – site covariates \(\color{Purple} w\) – observation covariate

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
The multinomial distribution

This is the first multivariate distribution we’ve covered. \[
  \{y_{1}, \dots, y_{K}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N, \{\pi_i, \dots, \pi_K\})
\]
The multinomial describes how \(N\) objects are distributed among \(K\) classes (also called bins, categories, etc).




Imagine \(N=20\) animals are studied for 1 year and there are 3 possible “fates” with associated probabilities: \(\Pr(\mathrm{survived})=0.5\), \(\Pr(\mathrm{depredated})=0.3\), \(\Pr(\mathrm{starved})=0.2\).
Here is one possible outcome:



N <- 20
pi <- c(survived=0.5, depredated=0.3, starved=0.2) ## Probs must sum to 1
t(rmultinom(n=1, size=N, prob=pi))                 ## Counts must sum to N

     survived depredated starved
[1,]       11          5       4

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Sampling methods

Benefits of the multinomial \(N\)-mixture model

Precision is typically better than binomial \(N\)-mixture models because there’s more information in the data.
Can be applied to data from many sampling designs, simply by changing how the \(\pi\) probabilities are computed.




Removal sampling \[
  {\pi(p)} = \{p, (1-p)p, (1-p)^2p, \dots, (1-p)^{K-1}p, (1-p)^K\}
\]
Double observer (independent observers) \[
  {\pi(p)} = \{p_1(1-p_2), (1-p_1)p_2, p_1p_2, (1-p_1)(1-p_2)\}
\]
Double observer (dependent observers) \[
  {\pi(p)} = \{p_1, (1-p_1)p_2, (1-p_1)(1-p_2)\}
\]

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Removal sampling

Removal sampling is often used in electrofishing studies.
A stream section is surveyed \(J\) times, fish are removed on each “pass”, and the rate of removal tells us about capture probability.





\(y_{ij}\) – number of individuals removed at site \(i\) on pass \(j\)
\(p\) – probability of catching an individual on a single pass






Description
Multinomial cell probability




Pr(first captured on first pass)
\(\pi_1 = p\)


Pr(first captured on second pass)
\(\pi_2 = (1-p)p\)


Pr(first captured on third pass)
\(\pi_3 = (1-p)(1-p)p\)


\(\cdots\)
\(\cdots\)


Pr(first captured on pass \(J\))
\(\pi_J = (1-p)^{J-1}p\)


Pr(not captured)
\(\pi_{J+1} = (1-p)^J\)

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Bayesian multinomial N-mixture models

There are several equivalent formulations of the multinomial that can be used to fit the model.

Conditional-on-\(N\), missing \(y_{iK}\) (Not possible in JAGS)
Conditional-on-\(N\), conditional on \(n_i=\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} y_{i,k}\)
Conditional-on-\(N\), sequential binomial
Marginalized \(N\)

These are just probability tricks that can affect MCMC performance. See AHM I for details. Here, we will focus on the second option.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Conditional-on-N and ni

We can break the problem down into two steps by conditioning on \(n_i\), the number of individuals captured at site \(i\):
\[
  n_i \sim \mathrm{Bin}(N_i, 1-\pi_K) \\
  \{y_{i,1}, \dots, y_{i,K-1}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_i, \{\pi_{i,1}, \dots, \pi_{i,K-1}\}/(1-\pi_K))
\]
Note that the modified cell probabilities still sum to 1.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Conditional-on-N and ni
removal-mod2.jag


model {

lambda.intercept ~ dunif(0, 5)
beta0 <- log(lambda.intercept)
beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5)

alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5)  
alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5)

for(i in 1:nSites) {
  log(lambda[i]) <- beta0 + beta1*streamDepth[i]
  N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])         # Latent local abundance
  logit(p[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha1*streamDepth[i]
  pi[i,1] <- p[i]               ## Pr(first captured in first pass)
  pi[i,2] <- (1-p[i])*p[i]      ## Pr(first captured in second pass)
  pi[i,3] <- (1-p[i])^2*p[i]    ## Pr(first captured in third pass)
  pi[i,4] <- (1-p[i])^3         ## Pr(not captured)
  n[i] ~ dbin(1-pi[i,4], N[i])  ## nCaptured at site i
  y[i,1:3] ~ dmulti(pi[i,1:3]/(1-pi[i,4]), n[i])
}

totalAbundance <- sum(N[1:nSites])

}

Two observers sample the same location at the same time, working independently.
After each survey, they compare notes and figure out which individual were detected by observer A only, B only, or by both.

section: Dependent double observer model in JAGS
text:
Dependent double observer model in JAGS
double-obs-dep.jag


model {

lambda ~ dunif(0, 20) # Prior on E(N)
p1 ~ dunif(0, 1)      # Prior on observer A detection prob
p2 ~ dunif(0, 1)      # Prior on observer B detection prob

# Multinomial cell probs
piAfirst <- c(p1, (1-p1)*p2, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) # When obs A goes first
piBfirst <- c(p2, (1-p2)*p1, (1-p1)*(1-p2)) # When obs B goes first

for(i in 1:nSites) {
  N[i] ~ dpois(lambda)         # Latent local abundance
  pi[i,1:3] <- ifelse(observer[i,1]==1, piAfirst, piBfirst)
  n[i] ~ dbin(1-pi[i,3], N[i])  ## nDetected at site i
  y[i,1:2] ~ dmulti(pi[i,1:2]/(1-pi[i,3]), n[i])
}

totalAbundance <- sum(N[1:nSites])

}

text:
Additional remarks on double observer models


In practice, there are often many observers on a project, even though only two survey at a time.


We can deal with this by including “observer ID” as an observation covariate. Everything else stays the same.


It can be hard to pull of the independent double observer method because observers often influence each other while working.


All of these methods require some sort of short-term individual identification of animals, even though they aren’t being marked.


If short-term individual ID isn’t possible, you could fall back on binomial \(N\)-mixture models.

Prior predictive recap

There are two common strategies for specifying priors:

Use uniform/flat priors to obtain results that will often be similar to likelihood-based methods.
Use priors that reflect available information.


The second approach can be used even if there isn’t much prior information available. Priors can allow for the possibility of being “surprised” by the data, but without putting most of the prior weight on extreme values.


Often, highly diffuse priors on the link scale result in most of the prior weight being on extreme values on the natural scale.


Prior predictive checks can be used to assess this possibility, and should be a standard component of Bayesian analysis.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Model selection

In scientific contexts, we want models that describe natural processes and allow us to evaluate hypotheses.


Models should be predictive, but they shouldn’t be crafted with the sole goal of prediction in mind.



Scientists typically don’t care about prediction if the model doesn’t help us learn about the processes that gave rise to the data.



Nonetheless, predictive performance is often the best way to compare models and avoid underfitting and overfitting.



Make sure the models being compared were motivated by clear hypotheses.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Model selection

Prediction accuracy increases with model complexity up to a point, until overfitting kicks in.

The best way to determine if a model is too simplistic or too complex is to compare predictions to new observations.


However, we rarely have the resources to collect additional data for the sake of evaluating predictive performance.


A cheaper (albeit less desirable) alternative is to use cross-validation:

Split data into K partitions
Fit model to the data in K-1 partitions
Predict the holdout partition




Information criteria like AIC and WAIC yield similar predictive rankings as cross-validation, but with less computation.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Model selection with AIC

Most information criteria (IC) take on a form like this: \[
  \mathrm{IC} = \mathrm{fit} + \mathrm{penalty}
\]
where fit describes the in-sample predictive accuracy and penalty describes model complexity.

In the case of Akaike’s “An Information Criterion”, which approximates leave-one-out cross validation, fit is described by the likelihood and the penalty is determined by the number of parameters: \[
  \mathrm{AIC} = -2 \log(L) + 2P
\] where \(L\) is the likelihood evaluated at the MLE and \(P\) is the number of parameters.


The lower the AIC, the better the out-of-sample predictive performance.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
WAIC

Watanabe’s widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) is a generalization of AIC suitable for Bayesian models.
As before, we have
\[
  \mathrm{WAIC} = \mathrm{fit} + \mathrm{penalty}
\]
The measure of fit in this case is the log-pointwise-predictive-density:


\[
   \mathrm{lppd} = \sum_{i=1}^M \log\left(\frac{1}{S} \sum_s p(y_i|\theta_s)\right)
\]
The penalty is proportional to the posterior variance: \[
  \mathrm{penalty} = \sum_{i=1}^M \mathrm{Var}(\log p(y_i|\theta_s)))
\]

WAIC

\[
  \mathrm{WAIC} = -2\left(\mathrm{lppd} - \sum_i \mathrm{Var}(\log p(y_i|\theta))\right)
\]

waic <- function(x) {
    ## Parameter names
    vars <- coda::varnames(x)
    ## Extract log-density of y at each site for each post sample
    ld.samples <- as.matrix(x[,grep("ld.y.dot", vars)])
    ## Compute log-pointwise-predictive-density
    lppd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(ld.samples))))
    ## Compute penalty
    penalty <- sum(apply(ld.samples, 2, var))
    ## Return WAIC
    return(-2*(lppd-penalty))
}

text:
Goodness-of-fit

Distributional assumptions determine the expected values and the expected variance of the random variables, including the data.

Overdispersion occurs when there is more variance in the data than expected by the model. Goodness-of-fit methods assess overdispersion and underdispersion.


If the model does not fit the data very well because of overdispersion, there are several remedial actions:

Scientific approach

Figure out why there is unexplained variation
Perhaps there were unmeasured covariates or you need a better process model

Statistical approach

Soak up variation with random effects
Use a different distribution (we’ll start here)

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Changing the distribution for \(N\)

Standard Poisson-binomial \(N\)-mixture model (without covariates): \[
  N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) \\
  y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_i, p)
\]

We can replace the Poisson distribution with other distributions that allow for greater variance in \(N\). Two common examples are the negative binomial: \[
    N_i \sim \mathrm{NegBin}(\lambda_i, \kappa)
\] where \(\lambda_i\) is the expected value of \(N\) and \(\kappa\) is the dispersion parameter.  


Another option is the zero-inflated Poisson:


\[
  N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i z_i) \\
  z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi)
\]

\[
  N_i \sim \mathrm{ZIPoisson}(\lambda_i,\psi)
\]

where \(\psi\) is the expected proportion of sites with excess zeros.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Simulating data from ZIP model

Zero-inflated Poisson model


\[
  N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i z_i) \\
  z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi)
\]

\[
  N_i \sim \mathrm{ZIPoisson}(\lambda_i,\psi)
\]

R code

nSites <- 20
nVisits <- 3
psi <- 0.5   # Proportion of extra-Poisson zeros
z <- rbinom(n=nSites, size=1, prob=psi) # Extra zeros
lam <- 5     # expected count when z=1
N <- rpois(n=nSites, lambda=lam*z)      # abundance at each site
p <- 0.5     # detection prob
y <- matrix(NA, nSites, nVisits)
for(i in 1:nSites) {
    y[i,] <- rbinom(n=nVisits, size=N[i], prob=p) # count data
}

In a Bayesian analysis, we can assess model fit using a posterior predictive check (PPC).

The PPC compares the posterior distribution of a fit statistic, to the posterior distribution of a fit statistic computed from simulated data.

beta3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5)

alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5)

for(i in 1:nSites) {
  elevation[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  utmN[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  utmE[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  log(lambda[i]) <- beta0 + beta1*elevation[i] + beta3*utmN[i]
  N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])         # Latent local abundance
  N.new[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])     # Predicted local abundance
  for(j in 1:nOccasions) {
    temp[i,j] ~ dnorm(0,1)
    logit(p[i,j]) <- alpha0 + alpha1*temp[i,j]
    y[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])              # Data
    resid[i,j] <- y[i,j]-N[i]*p[i,j]         # Residual
    y.new[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N.new[i])          # Predicted data
    resid.new[i,j] <- y.new[i,j]-N.new[i]*p[i,j] # Predicted residual
  }
}
SSE <- sum(resid^2)             # Fit stat
SSE.new <- sum(resid.new^2)     # Predicted fit stat

totalAbundance <- sum(N[1:nSites])

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Motivation

We often want to do logistic regression, but the data are subject to measurement error.


Specifically, wildlife data are often fraught with false negatives (ie, the species was there but we didn’t detect it).



Ignoring this source of measurement error can result in misleading inferences.

Occupancy will be under-estimated
Habitat associations may be incorrect

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Accounting for detection probability

The model for the state process is the same as logistic regression:
\[
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathrm{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots \\
    z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi_i)
  \end{gather*}
\]

Model for the observation process conditional on the state process:
\[
\begin{gather*}
    \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x_{ij1} + \alpha_2 x_{ij2} + \cdots \\
    y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i\times p_{ij})
  \end{gather*}
\]

\(\psi_i\) – probability that the species occurs at site \(i\)
\(z_i\) – binary presence/absence variable at site \(i\)
\(p_{ij}\) – probability of detecting the species at site \(i\) on occasion \(j\)
\(y_{ij}\) – binary detection/non-detection data

\[
  \begin{gather*}
    z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi) \\

  \end{gather*}
\]


\(\psi\) – probability that the species occurs at site \(i\)
\(z_i\) – binary presence/absence variable at site \(i\)
\(p\) – probability of detecting the species at site \(i\) on occasion \(j\)
\(y_{ij}\) – binary detection/non-detection data

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Distance sampling overview
Distance sampling is one of the oldest wildlife sampling methods.

It’s based on the simple idea that detection probability should decline with distance between an animal and a transect.


If we can estimate the function describing how \(p\) declines with distance \(x\), we can estimate abundance…


… if certain assumptions hold, as always.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Distance sampling overview

The simplest estimator of abundance is \[
  \hat{N} = \frac{n}{\hat{p}}
\] where \(n\) is the number of individuals detected, \(p\) is detection probability, and \(E(n)=Np\).

In distance sampling, detection probability is a function of distance, rather than a constant, such that all individuals have unique detection probabilities.


As a result, we have to replace \(p\) with average detection probability: \[
  \hat{N} = \frac{n}{\hat{\bar{p}}}
\]


How do we compute average detection probability (\(\bar{p}\))?

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Detection functions

To estimate average detection probability (\(\bar{p}\)), we need:

A detection function \(g(x)\) describing how \(p\) declines with distance.
A probability distribution \(p(x)\) describing the distances of all animals (detected and not detected).

The most common detection functions are:



Detection function
\(g(x)\)




Half normal
\(\exp(-x^2 / (2\sigma^2))\)


Negative exponential
\(\exp(-x/\sigma)\)


Hazard rate
\(1-\exp(-(x/a)^{-b})\)

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Half-normal

\[
    g(x,\sigma) = \exp(-x^2/(2\sigma^2))
\]

sigma1 <- 25; sigma2 <- 50
plot(function(x) exp(-x^2/(2*sigma1^2)), from=0, to=100, 
     xlab="Distance (x)", ylab="Detection probability (p)")
plot(function(x) exp(-x^2/(2*sigma2^2)), from=0, to=100, add=TRUE, col=4)
legend(70, 1, c("sigma=25", "sigma=50"), lty=1, col=c("black","blue"))

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Negative exponential

\[
    g(x,\sigma) = \exp(-x/\sigma)
\]

sigma1 <- 25; sigma2 <- 50
plot(function(x) exp(-x/sigma1), from=0, to=100, 
     xlab="Distance (x)", ylab="Detection probability (p)")
plot(function(x) exp(-x/sigma2), from=0, to=100, add=TRUE, col=4)
legend(70, 1, c("sigma=25", "sigma=50"), lty=1, col=c("black","blue"))

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Hazard rate

\[
    g(x,a,b) = 1-\exp(-(x/a)^{-b})
\]

a1 <- 25; a2 <- 50; b1 <- 2; b2 <- 10
plot(function(x) 1-exp(-(x/a1)^(-b1)), from=0, to=100, 
     xlab="Distance (x)", ylab="Detection probability (p)", ylim=0:1)
plot(function(x) 1-exp(-(x/a2)^(-b2)), from=0, to=100, add=TRUE, col=4)
legend(70, 1, c("a=25, b=2", "a=50, b=10"), lty=1, col=c("black","blue"))

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Average detection probability

Regardless of the chosen detection function, average detection probability is defined as: \[
     \bar{p} = \int_{0}^{B} g(x)p(x) \; \mathrm{d}x
\] where \(B\) is the width of the transect.

All that remains is the specification of \(p(x)\), the distribution of distances (between animals and the transect).


To understand why \(p(x)\) is needed, think about it this way:

If most animals are close to the transect, \(\bar{p}\) would be high
If most animals are far from the transect, \(\bar{p}\) would be low

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
section: What should we use for p(x)?
text:
What should we use for p(x)?

What distribution should we use for the distances between animals and transects?

In line-transect sampling, it is often assumed that animals are uniformly distributed with respect to the transect.

Consequently, \(p(x) = 1/B\), where \(x\) is the perpendicular distance between animal and transect
This is guaranteed by random transect placement
Can also be justified if animals are neither attracted to the transects or avoid them.



In point-transect sampling, we make the same assumptions, but we recognize that area increases with distance from a point.

Consequently, \(p(x) = 2x/B^2\) (see pg. 408 in AHM)
Here, \(x\) is the radial distance to an animal

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Conventional vs hierarchical distance sampling

Conventional distance sampling

Focus is on estimation of detection function parameters and density
No model for spatial variation in density
Data are individual-level distances
We’ll deal with CDS in more depth as a prelude to spatial-capture recapture


Hierarchical distance sampling

Focus is on estimation of detection function parameters and spatial variation in abundance/density
Data are counts of individuals in each distance bin
Multinomial \(N\)-mixture model with a unique function for computing the multinomial cell probabilities

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Hierarchical distance sampling

State model (with Poisson assumption) \[
    \mathrm{log}(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 {w_{i1}} +
    \beta_2 {w_{i2}} + \cdots \\
    N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
\]
Observation model \[
    \mathrm{log}(\sigma_{i}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 {w_{i1}}
    + \alpha_2 {w_{i3}} + \cdots \\
    \{y_{i1}, \dots, y_{iK}\}  \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N_i,
    \pi(x, \sigma_i))
\]



\(\lambda_i\) – Expected value of abundance at site \(i\)  \(N_i\) – Realized value of abundance at site \(i\)  \(\sigma_{i}\) – Scale parameter of detection function \(g(x)\) at site \(i\)  \(\pi(x,\sigma_i)\) – Function computing multinomial cell probs  \(y_{ij}\) – count for distance bin \(j\) (final count is unobserved)  \(w_1\), \(w_2\), \(w_3\) – site covariates

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
section: Multinomial cell probs for point transects
text:
Multinomial cell probs for point transects

Definitions needed for computing \(\bar{p}\) and multinomial cell probabilities.

\(y_{ij}\) – number of individuals detected at site \(i\) in bin \(j\)
\(\sigma_i\) – scale parameter of detection function \(g(x)\)
\(b_1, \dots, b_J\) – Distance break points defining \(J\) distance intervals
\(\bar{p}_j\) – Average detection probability in distance interval \(j\).
\(\psi_j\) – Probability of occuring in distance band \(j\)










Description
Multinomial cell probability




Pr(occurs and detected in first distance bin)
\(\pi_1 = \psi_1\bar{p}_1\)


Pr(occurs and detected in second distance bin)
\(\pi_2 = \psi_2\bar{p}_2\)


\(\cdots\)
\(\cdots\)


Pr(occurs and detected in last distance bin)
\(\pi_J = \psi_J\bar{p}_J\)


Pr(not detected)
\(\pi_{K} = 1-\sum_{j=1}^J \pi_j\)

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Point transects, no covariates

Abundance

B <- 100; Area <- pi*B^2/1e4   ## plot radius (B) and area in ha
nSites <- 100; lambda1 <- 0.9  ## Expected value of density
N3 <- rpois(n=nSites, lambda=lambda1*Area)

Multinomial cell probabilities

J <- 5                     # distance bins
sigma <- 50                # scale parameter
b <- seq(0, B, length=J+1) # distance break points
area <- pi*b^2             # area of each circle
psi <- (area[-1]-area[-(J+1)]) / area[J+1]
pbar3 <- numeric(J)        # average detection probability
pi3 <- numeric(J+1)        # multinomial cell probs
for(j in 1:J) {
    pbar3[j] <- integrate(function(x) exp(-x^2/(2*sigma^2))*x,
                          lower=b[j], upper=b[j+1])$value *
                          (2*pi/diff(area)[j])
    pi3[j] <- pbar3[j]*psi[j] }; pi3[J+1] <- 1-sum(pi3[1:J])

Detections in each distance interval

y3.all <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=J+1)
for(i in 1:nSites) {
    y3.all[i,] <- rmultinom(n=1, size=N3[i], prob=pi3)    }
y3 <- y3.all[,1:J]  ## Drop final cell

elevation <- rnorm(nSites)  
beta0 <- 2; beta1 <- 1
lambda4 <- exp(beta0 + beta1*elevation)   # E(density)
N4 <- rpois(n=nSites, lambda=lambda4*Area)

Multinomial cell probabilities

alpha0 <- 3; alpha1 <- -0.5
sigma4 <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1*noise)
pi4 <- matrix(NA, nSites, J+1) # multinomial cell probs
for(i in 1:nSites) {

          lower=b[j], upper=b[j+1])$value*(2*pi/diff(area)[j])*psi[j] }
  pi4[i,J+1] <- 1-sum(pi4[i,1:J]) }

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Overview


Explaining variation in occupancy and detection probability with covariates is central to reliable prediction and scientific investigation. 


In static occupancy models, there are two types of covariates:

Site covariates vary among sites but not among occasions.
Observation covariates may vary among sites and occasions




In both cases, covariates can be continuous or categorical.


Observation covariates cannot be used to describe variation in occupancy because occupancy is assumed to be constant over time.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Covariates

State model \[
  \small
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathrm{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} +
    \beta_2 {\color{blue} x_{i2}} + \cdots \\
    z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi_i)
  \end{gather*}
\]
Observation model \[
  \small
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}}
    + \alpha_2 {\color{Coral} w_{ij}} + \cdots \\
    y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i\times p_{ij})
  \end{gather*}
\]
\(\color{blue} x_1\) and \(\color{blue} x_2\) are site covariates.  Examples: elevation, forest cover, distance to water.
\(\color{Coral} w\) is an observation covariate.  Examples: time of day, observer, wind.

                      replace=TRUE),

tempHot <- ifelse(temp=="Hot", 1, 0)      # Dummy variable

beta0 <- 5; beta1 <- -0.001; beta2 <- 0
psi <- plogis(beta0 + beta1*elev + beta2*forest)
alpha0 <- -6.5; alpha1 <- 0.001; alpha2 <- 2

y <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits)

Summary of static occupancy models

Assumptions are made explicit by the model description, but it’s worth emphasizing that:

Occupancy is assumed to remain constant at each site during the sampling period.
The definition of a ‘site’ is critical, but can difficult in some situations, such as in camera studies.
Abundance is assumed to be unimportant.
Observations are assumed to be independent, conditional on latent variables and covariates.


These assumptions can be relaxed if we have enough data.

Dynamic occupancy models

Occupancy evolves as a function of local colonization and extinction.

\(N\)-mixture models

Focus is on local abundance, rather than presence/absence.





We’ll talk more about design issues later.

Simple linear regression
Simple linear regression is the most basic linear model. \[
    \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \qquad \qquad
    y_i \sim \mathrm{Norm}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)
\]



\(y\) is variously called:

response variable
outcome variable
dependent variable




It’s worse for \(x\)

predictor variable
explanatory variable
independent variable
covariate, exposure, etc…




We observe \(x\) and \(y\). The expected value of \(y_i\) is \(\mu_i\).

We’d like to estimate \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), called the “coefficients”.

A residual is \(\varepsilon_i=y_i-\mu_i\).
\(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the residuals.

A more general depiction of linear models:
\[
  \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} \\
  y_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Interpreting the \(\beta\) coefficients
You need to be able to interpret the \(\beta\) coefficients for any model that you fit to your data.

A linear model might have dozens of continuous and categorical predictors variables, with dozens of associated \(\beta\) coefficients.

Linear models can also include polynomial terms and interactions.

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Interpreting the \(\beta\)’s
The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is the expected value of \(y\), when all \(x=0\).



If \(x_1\) is a continuous explanatory variable:

\(\beta_1\) can usually be interpreted as a slope parameter.
In this case, \(\beta_1\) is the change in \(y\) resulting from a 1 unit change in \(x_1\) (while holding the other predictors constant).

title: Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
text:
Interpreting \(\beta\)’s for categorical explanatory variables
Things are more complicated for categorical explanatory variables (i.e., factors) because they must be converted to dummy variables. There are many ways of creating dummy variables. In R, the default method for creating dummy variables from unordered factors works like this:

One level of the factor is treated as a reference level.
The reference level is associated with the intercept.
The \(\beta\) coefficients for the other levels of the factor are differences from the reference level.

Bayesian Poisson regression
The model is in a text file named glm.jag

model {

    # Priors
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) ## Normal prior with mean=0, variance=10
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

    ## Model for the data
    for(i in 1:n) {
      lambda[i] <- exp(beta0 + beta1*x[i])
      y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    }

}

jd.glm <- list(x=x, y=y, n=length(y))
